n: This heading introduces the whole book. Isaiah prophesied in Jerusalem for roughly forty years, under four kings of Judah, during the rise of the Assyrian Empire (about 740–700 BC).

f.g: Hebrew ḥazon — a revelation seen by a prophet; here a title for his whole collection of prophecies.

n: Like a lawyer calling witnesses, Isaiah summons heaven and earth to hear the Lord’s case. God is a loving Father who raised His children, yet they rebelled against Him.

f.w: Hear, O heavens, and give ear, O earth
I have nourished and brought up children

n: Even farm animals know who feeds them, but Israel does not recognize or think about the God who cares for them. Their forgetfulness is worse than an animal’s.

f.g: Feeding trough or manger.
Understand or pay attention.

n: Isaiah mourns over a nation weighed down by sin. They have abandoned the Lord and turned their backs on Him. “Holy One of Israel” is Isaiah’s favorite title for God.

f.g: Used about 25 times in Isaiah and often in the Book of Mormon (e.g. 2 Nephi 9:41).
Turned away; become estranged.

n: Why keep rebelling and getting hurt? The nation is like a body sick from head to heart. Their punishments haven’t brought them back.

f.g: Struck, punished.
Sick, weak.

n: The nation is covered in untreated wounds from head to foot. No one has cleaned, bandaged, or soothed them — a picture of a people who refuse healing.

f.g: Fresh, open wounds.
Softened or soothed.

n: Isaiah describes the land devastated by foreign invaders. Many scholars connect this with Assyria’s invasion of Judah under Sennacherib in 701 BC, when many towns were destroyed.
Jerusalem is left alone like a flimsy watchman’s hut in a field after harvest — isolated and vulnerable, surrounded by enemies.

f.g: A poetic name for Jerusalem and its people.
A temporary shelter for a field watchman.

n: If the Lord had not spared a small remnant, Judah would have been wiped out like Sodom and Gomorrah. The idea of a faithful remnant runs through Isaiah.

f.g: Jehovah of armies — Lord over the hosts of heaven and earth.

n: The Lord now speaks, shockingly calling Judah’s leaders and people “Sodom” and “Gomorrah” because of their wickedness.

f.g: Hebrew torah — instruction or teaching.

n: God says He is sick of their many sacrifices. He did not reject sacrifice itself, but sacrifice offered without repentance and righteous living.

f.g: What good is it?

n: Who asked them to trample through the temple courts with empty worship? Coming to the temple without changed hearts is mere trespassing.

f.g: Trample the temple courtyards.

n: Stop bringing meaningless offerings. Even holy days and gatherings become offensive when mixed with wickedness.

f.g: Empty, worthless offerings.
I cannot endure or put up with.

n: God says their festivals have become a burden He is tired of carrying. Ritual without righteousness wearies Him.

f.g: Monthly festivals at the start of each lunar month (Numbers 28:11).

n: When they raise their hands to pray, God will not listen, because their hands are stained with violence and injustice.

f.g: The ancient posture of prayer, with palms lifted up.

n: The cure begins here: wash, become clean, and stop doing evil. These verses outline repentance.
Repentance includes actively doing good: seeking justice, helping the oppressed, defending orphans and widows. Religion must reach the vulnerable.

f.g: Defend the cause of the orphan.

n: One of scripture’s most beloved invitations: the Lord invites His people to come and settle the matter with Him. Even the deepest-stained sins can be made pure through His mercy, which Latter-day Saints understand as the Atonement of Jesus Christ.

f.g: Settle the case together, as in a court.
A deep red dye that was almost impossible to wash out.

n: Those who are willing and obedient will enjoy the blessings of the land. Both desire and action matter.
But those who refuse and rebel will fall by the sword. The choice and its consequences are theirs.

f.w: the mouth of the LORD hath spoken it

n: Isaiah laments that Jerusalem, once faithful like a loyal wife, has become unfaithful like a prostitute. Where justice once lived, now there are murderers.

f.g: A common prophetic image for spiritual unfaithfulness to God (Jeremiah 3:1; Hosea 2).

n: Their silver has become worthless slag and their wine watered down. What was once pure is now corrupted and diluted.

f.g: The impurities skimmed off when refining metal.

n: Judah’s leaders are rebels who partner with thieves and love bribes. They ignore orphans and widows instead of protecting them.

f.g: Loves bribes.

n: God, using three solemn titles, announces He will deal with His enemies — here, the wicked among His own people.

f.g: A title echoing Jacob’s blessing (Genesis 49:24).
Get relief from; settle accounts with.

n: Like a refiner, God will purify Jerusalem, melting away its impurities. His judgment is meant to cleanse, not merely destroy.

f.g: An alloy or impurity mixed with silver.

n: Afterward God will restore honest judges and counselors, and Jerusalem will again be called the city of righteousness. Latter-day Saints also see a latter-day fulfillment in a redeemed Zion.
Zion will be redeemed through justice, and those who return to God through righteousness.

f.g: Those who return or repent.

n: But rebels and sinners who abandon the Lord will be destroyed together.
They will be ashamed of the sacred oak groves and gardens where they worshiped idols. Pagan fertility worship was often held in such places.

f.g: Sacred trees used in idol worship (Hosea 4:13).
Put to shame.

n: The idolaters will become like the very things they trusted — a withering oak and a dried-up garden.
The “strong” who trust in themselves will be like dry kindling, their own deeds the spark that ignites them. Sin carries the seeds of its own destruction.

f.g: Flax fibers that burn instantly.
Better “his work” — his own deeds set him on fire.
